A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FlipAttack and contain readable main text, figures, tables, mathematical definitions, and complete appendices. Retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack evaluations on eight LLMs, guard-model tests, ablations, defense experiments, and analyses of perplexity and flipping accuracy.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds tokenization measurements, system-prompt ablations, and white-box source-model checks.

M1.justification: The four flipping modes and four guidance variants remain. v2 reports a limited prompt-level revision: condition B, called the current method and used in Table 1, removes an added system prompt relative to A, whose scores match v1. However, the retained prompt templates do not identify precisely what was removed.

E1.justification: The AdvBench, StrongREJECT, JailbreakBench-derived, and Alpaca safe data coverage is retained. v2 adds a restricted interface scenario in Table 17, moving attack instructions entirely into the user prompt, extending evaluation beyond the previously reported system-channel configuration.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain the same 15 competing attacks, and Figure 6 retains PAIR, auto obfuscation, auto payload splitting, disemvowel, and ROT13. The added 13B-source AutoDAN experiment changes the source-model setting of an existing comparator.

E3.justification: v2 associates its headline results with the revised B prompt condition in Table 13. Added protocols test system-to-user prompt placement, direct-source white-box success, AutoDAN transfer from a 13B source, and token counts across tokenizers. The core AdvBench sample counts and ASR metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's mode, guidance, defense, and case analyses, v2 adds tokenization analysis (Table 4), two system-prompt controls (Tables 13 and 17), and white-box source-performance and source-size checks (Tables 12 and 14). These substantially expand investigation of prompt dependence and baseline transferability. The original flipping-mode analysis is retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: Both versions report descriptive perplexity means and standard deviations without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's token-count mean and standard deviation add descriptive results without establishing a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes FlipAttack's mean ASR from 81.80% to 78.97% and GPT-4o ASR from 98.08% to 90.77%; v2 Table 13 associates these values with different prompt conditions, so they do not establish same-setting deterioration. Table 7's mean changes from 82.00% to 77.00%. New control results and revised category and ablation plots further change the empirical record.

T1.justification: The attack mapping, flipping definitions, and demonstration construction remain unchanged, with no new theorem, proof, or derivation. v2's threat-model paragraph summarizes system/user-prompt access already documented in v1's templates rather than introducing a substantively different formal assumption.

C1.justification: The single-query attack, average superiority, and approximately 98% guard-bypass claims remain. v2 replaces the abstract's approximately 98% GPT-4o headline with 78.97% average ASR across eight LLMs and reduces the introductory advantage over the runner-up from 25.16 to 22.33 percentage points.

C2.justification: v2 adds token-fragmentation and error-propagation explanations in Section 4.3, plus interpretations of system-channel vulnerability and comparison fairness in Appendix A.2. The three existing limitations, including weaker effectiveness against reasoning models such as o1, are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit white-box baseline repository links and states that their supplied hyperparameters were used (Table 11), tabulates token/GPU costs (Table 16), and reports PyRIT integration. Hardware, API sources, and model-specific flipping configurations remain substantially unchanged; the revised B prompt is insufficiently specified.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially revised: discussions and citations concerning PGD attacks, AdvPrompter, many-shot jailbreaking, and other approaches are removed, while reasoning safeguards such as GuardReasoner and GuardReasoner-VL and broader recent safety literature are added. The central positioning around efficient single-query attacks remains.

P1.justification: The detailed appendix survey is condensed and rewritten into Section 2, the separate mechanism discussion is folded into Section 3.1, and the flipping-mode ablation moves to the appendix. Widespread terminology changes replace noise with perturbation, prose is compressed, and threat-model and impact-statement passages are added.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from one-column to two-column formatting, with extensive resizing and repositioning of displays. Seven tables are added, while existing tables and figures are relocated or renumbered. The flipping-accuracy table moves to the appendix, and the method diagram's terminology is updated.

improvement.justification: The added source-model checks and system/user-prompt ablations provide useful evidence about transferability and dependence on privileged instructions that v1 lacked. These gains are limited by inadequate specification of the revised B prompt, unreconciled performance summaries such as Tables 1 and 16, and a new impact statement that misleadingly describes the contribution as a guard model.
